This is my latest post on Patreon. Go sign up for more stuff like this! 

From Enemies to Allies to Something More

In March of 2026, X's AI-powered translation feature got a tweak, and the platform's recommendation algorithm shifted in a way that broke down one of the oldest barriers in the internet age: the language wall between American and Japanese users.

It started with a Japanese post about U.S. soldiers cooking bacon at a Japanese barbecue restaurant. Americans saw it. They loved it. Japanese users started showing up in American feeds talking about Southern BBQ, smoked brisket, Texas culture. Americans started flooding Japanese feeds with their own enthusiasm. Within days, millions of people on both sides of the Pacific were discovering something that probably shouldn't have surprised anyone: we actually like each other. A lot.

The left didn't know what to do with it. It didn't fit the narrative. Two cultures with genuine warmth for each other, no DEI framework required, no UN resolution necessary. Just people realizing they had more in common than 80 years of ocean and language barrier had let them see.

But this didn't come from nowhere. The affinity was always there. It was built, slowly and sometimes painfully, out of one of the most unlikely partnerships in modern history. Understanding how we got here tells you a lot about where we're going, and what it means for Asia, especially those watching from Beijing.

THE RUBBLE

In August 1945, the United States dropped two atomic bombs on Japan and accepted its unconditional surrender. The American view of Japan at that moment was not complicated: a fanatical enemy that had attacked without warning, that had fought to the last man on every island in the Pacific, that would need to be fundamentally remade before it could rejoin the community of nations.

The Japanese view of America was harder to read from the outside. Here was the nation that had just incinerated Hiroshima and Nagasaki. And yet, when General Douglas MacArthur arrived in Japan as Supreme Commander of the Allied Powers, he was not met with the kind of guerrilla resistance that American planners had feared. The surrender held.

MacArthur set up headquarters in the Daiichi Insurance building, directly across from the Imperial Palace, and got to work redesigning a country. What followed was one of the stranger episodes in the history of great power politics: a five-star American general, a man defined by military command, writing a pacifist constitution for a defeated enemy.

Article 9 of Japan's 1947 constitution, drafted under MacArthur's occupation, renounced war as a sovereign right and prohibited Japan from maintaining war potential. A military man had written a document forbidding military power. The clause's exact origin is disputed, but its effect was not: Japan would rebuild under an American security umbrella, with someone else responsible for its defense.

The decision to keep Emperor Hirohito on the throne was equally calculated. American planners understood that prosecuting or removing the emperor would radicalize the Japanese population in ways that could make occupation unmanageable. Hirohito stayed, stripped of power but present, a symbol of continuity that made an extraordinary national humiliation bearable. The occupation, remarkably, did not produce the lasting resentment that Versailles had produced in Germany a generation earlier.

THE COLD WAR PIVOT

Whatever the occupation's idealism, what happened next was driven by hard geopolitics.

In June 1950, North Korea invaded South Korea. Overnight, Japan stopped being a defeated enemy and became an indispensable forward operating base. The United States needed Japan. That changed everything.

The Security Treaty between the United States and Japan was signed on September 8, 1951, the same day as the San Francisco Peace Treaty ending World War II in the Pacific. The arrangement was asymmetric by design: the United States would station forces in Japan and guarantee its security; Japan would host those forces and focus its national energy on economic rebuilding rather than military competition.

What followed is sometimes called the Japanese economic miracle, and the numbers are genuinely extraordinary. Japan's defense spending was capped at roughly 1% of GDP under the pacifist constitution, freeing enormous resources for industrial investment. Between 1953 and 1965, Japan's GDP expanded at rates that stunned the world. By the late 1960s, a country that had been bombed into rubble had become the second-largest economy on earth.

The arrangement suited both sides. Japan got security and market access. America got a stable, prosperous ally in a strategically critical location. The Cold War logic was simple: a strong Japan was a buffer against Soviet and Chinese communist expansion in Asia.

Underneath the surface, tensions existed. Japan's nationalist right never fully accepted the pacifist constitution as legitimate, viewing Article 9 as an imposition by a foreign occupier rather than a genuine expression of Japanese values. Rearmament debates simmered continuously. The Japan Self-Defense Forces, formally established in 1954, were a military in everything but official designation, constrained by constitutional limits but growing steadily in capability.

GROWING TOGETHER

The 1980s brought friction. Japan's economic success had become so overwhelming that American politicians and commentators began treating it as a threat. Trade wars erupted over automobiles, semiconductors, and electronics. Books with titles like "Japan as Number One" and "The Japan That Can Say No" captured an anxiety that Japan was winning an economic war while the United States footed the bill for its defense.

That anxiety turned out to be misplaced. The threats never materialized into the permanent Japanese economic dominance that American pundits feared. More importantly, the alliance held through all of it. Shared strategic interest and genuine cultural exchange proved more durable than trade disagreements.

The Self-Defense Forces continued their quiet evolution. Japan built one of the most capable naval forces in Asia, developed advanced air power, and accumulated expertise that made it a serious military actor while maintaining the constitutional fiction of non-offensive defense. By the time the Cold War ended in 1991, Japan had a military that looked, trained, and equipped itself like a real one.

The end of the Cold War did not end the alliance. China filled the vacuum that the Soviet Union left, and the geographic logic that made Japan essential in 1950 remained as compelling as ever.

THE RIGHT IN JAPAN AND THE RIGHT IN AMERICA

Here is what the viral X moment in March 2026 revealed that nobody in the mainstream press wanted to acknowledge: the cultural affinity between Americans and Japanese runs deep, and it tracks most naturally along conservative lines in both countries.

Japan's nationalist right is not a fringe movement. Nippon Kaigi, the country's most influential nationalist organization, counts roughly 250 members of the Diet (Japan's parliament, the equivalent of the U.S. Congress) among its affiliates, predominantly from the Liberal Democratic Party. Its stated goals include restoring national pride, revising the pacifist constitution, and preserving Japanese cultural identity against both domestic diffusion and external pressure. Shinzo Abe, Japan's longest-serving prime minister, was among its most prominent supporters, along with multiple current and former prime ministers and cabinet ministers.

The agenda should sound familiar. Restore national pride. Skepticism toward multilateral institutions. Defense of cultural continuity. Opposition to a domestic left that views any expression of national identity as suspect. The LDP's dominance of Japanese politics for most of the postwar period reflects a country that, like America, has a durable conservative majority that the globalist left has never successfully displaced.

The Abe-Trump relationship was not an accident of personal chemistry. It reflected something real. When Trump visited Japan in 2019, Abe organized a sumo tournament and a round of golf. They looked like two men who actually liked each other, because they did, because they understood each other's political project. Two leaders from two countries where the right had prevailed against a globalizing consensus that had declared nationalism obsolete.

Then came July 8, 2022. Shinzo Abe was shot and killed while giving a campaign speech in Nara. The assassin was Tetsuya Yamagami, a man who had spent years consumed by a grudge against the Unification Church, which he blamed for destroying his family financially. He viewed Abe as the Church's most prominent political ally and targeted him for that reason. Yamagami later pleaded guilty to murder.

The reaction in America, particularly on the right, was genuine grief. Abe wasn't just a foreign leader who had been friendly with Trump. He was understood as a kindred spirit, someone fighting the same cultural and ideological battle in his own country. The memes that followed said as much. After the Butler assassination attempt on Trump in July 2024, one of the most viral images on X was Abe's spirit reaching down from heaven to deflect the bullet. The joke was dark, but the feeling underneath it was real: American conservatives had genuinely mourned Abe, felt his loss personally, and the image of him protecting Trump from beyond captured something true about how the right in both countries saw each other.

That kinship didn't disappear with Abe. Japan's current prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, is herself a Nippon Kaigi member and one of the most prominent figures in Japan's nationalist right. When she visited the White House in March 2026, the meeting was congenial and forward-looking. Then a Japanese reporter asked Trump why he hadn't briefed allied nations before the Iran strikes. Trump's answer was immediate: "Why didn't you tell ME about Pearl Harbor?"

The chattering class erupted. Reckless. Offensive. Diplomatically disastrous. Takaichi smiled. Japan didn't take it as an insult, because it wasn't one. A Japanese citizen named captain S.O., writing on X the next day, put it better than any American commentator managed to: "Trump's Pearl Harbor joke wasn't an insult. It was the key that finally unlocked something buried deep in the Japanese soul. For 80 long years, we've carried" the weight of that defeat, of occupation, of being a nation that wasn't quite allowed to stand on its own. Trump's joke, directed at a Japanese reporter, sitting next to a Japanese prime minister, treated Japan as an equal, a country with its own complicated history that two adults could acknowledge and laugh about together. That's not how you talk to a vassal. That's how you talk to a friend.

Both rights share something the international left cannot stand: the belief that nations are real, that cultures are worth preserving, that sovereignty is not a relic but a necessity. Both are in direct confrontation with movements that view national identity as inherently dangerous and cultural preservation as indistinguishable from chauvinism. The affinity that showed up on X last month is the popular expression of something that has been visible at the leadership level for years.

WHERE IT GOES FROM HERE

Japan is rearming, and this time it is not gradual or symbolic.

In December 2022, Prime Minister Fumio Kishida announced a five-year defense buildup program targeting 2% of GDP in defense spending, a target previously associated with NATO membership requirements. Japan's fiscal year 2026 defense budget is on track to exceed $70 billion, making it one of the largest defense budgets in the world. The country has acquired Tomahawk cruise missiles from the United States, developing a counterstrike capability that would have been unthinkable under any previous interpretation of Article 9.

The constitutional debate is no longer academic. Revision of Article 9 has majority support within the LDP and has moved from taboo to active political discussion. Japan is not yet a fully rearmed power, but the direction is unmistakable.

A Japan that can project force changes the entire strategic geometry of Asia. South Korea, which has its own complicated history with Japan, has to recalculate. The Philippines, which is deepening its alliance with both the United States and Japan in response to Chinese pressure in the South China Sea, gains a more capable partner. Taiwan, whose survival depends on regional deterrence holding, gains another piece in a more credible defensive arrangement.

For China, this is close to a nightmare scenario. Beijing's strategic calculation has long rested on the assumption that the American-led security architecture in Asia was fragile, dependent on American willingness to bear costs that domestic politics might eventually make unacceptable. A rearmed Japan with genuine offensive capability, embedded in a network of aligned regional partners who have stopped hedging between Washington and Beijing, changes that calculation significantly.

The Pax Americana, in the form of a single hegemon guaranteeing everyone's security at American taxpayer expense, may indeed be contracting. What is replacing it is not a vacuum. It is a network of sovereign nations with aligned interests, capable of their own defense, choosing cooperation based on shared values rather than dependence on a single patron. That is not weakness. That is a more durable arrangement.

WHAT CHINA IS WATCHING

There is a reason China has been quiet about the American-Japanese social media moment, even as its state media works overtime to characterize every aspect of the US-Japan alliance as militarist aggression. Popular affinity between two democratic publics is exactly the kind of soft power that authoritarian systems cannot manufacture.

The US-Japan alliance started as an occupation. It became a security arrangement. It became an economic partnership. It became something neither side fully planned for: a genuine friendship between two peoples with profoundly different histories, different languages, different cultures, who discovered, decade by decade and now post by post, that they see the world in compatible ways.

What the right in both countries understands, and what the internationalist left has never quite grasped, is that alliances built on genuine affinity and shared values outlast alliances built on multilateral frameworks and bureaucratic process. NATO has a charter. The US-Japan alliance has something older and more durable: two peoples who have decided they like each other.

China is watching. It should be paying attention.

Between 1953 and 1965, Japan's GDP expanded at rates that stunned the world. By the late 1960s, a country that had been bombed into rubble had become the second-largest economy on earth. The arrangement suited both sides. Japan got security and market access. America got a stable, prosperous ally in a strategically critical location. The Cold War logic was simple: a strong Japan was a buffer against Soviet and Chinese communist expansion in Asia. Underneath the surface, tensions existed. Japan's nationalist right never fully accepted the pacifist constitution as legitimate, viewing Article 9 as an imposition by a foreign occupier rather than a genuine expression of Japanese values. Rearmament debates simmered continuously. The Japan Self-Defense Forces, formally established in 1954, were a military in everything but official designation, constrained by constitutional limits but growing steadily in capability. GROWING TOGETHER The 1980s brought friction. Japan's economic success had become so overwhelming that American politicians and commentators began treating it as a threat. Trade wars erupted over automobiles, semiconductors, and electronics. Books with titles like "Japan as Number One" and "The Japan That Can Say No" captured an anxiety that Japan was winning an economic war while the United States footed the bill for its defense. That anxiety turned out to be misplaced. The threats never materialized into the permanent Japanese economic dominance that American pundits feared. More importantly, the alliance held through all of it. Shared strategic interest and genuine cultural exchange proved more durable than trade disagreements. The Self-Defense Forces continued their quiet evolution. Japan built one of the most capable naval forces in Asia, developed advanced air power, and accumulated expertise that made it a serious military actor while maintaining the constitutional fiction of non-offensive defense. By the time the Cold War ended in 1991, Japan had a military that looked, trained, and equipped itself like a real one. The end of the Cold War did not end the alliance. China filled the vacuum that the Soviet Union left, and the geographic logic that made Japan essential in 1950 remained as compelling as ever. THE RIGHT IN JAPAN AND THE RIGHT IN AMERICA Here is what the viral X moment in March 2026 revealed that nobody in the mainstream press wanted to acknowledge: the cultural affinity between Americans and Japanese runs deep, and it tracks most naturally along conservative lines in both countries. Japan's nationalist right is not a fringe movement. Nippon Kaigi, the country's most influential nationalist organization, counts roughly 250 members of the Diet (Japan's parliament, the equivalent of the U.S. Congress) among its affiliates, predominantly from the Liberal Democratic Party. Its stated goals include restoring national pride, revising the pacifist constitution, and preserving Japanese cultural identity against both domestic diffusion and external pressure. Shinzo Abe, Japan's longest-serving prime minister, was among its most prominent supporters, along with multiple current and former prime ministers and cabinet ministers. The agenda should sound familiar. Restore national pride. Skepticism toward multilateral institutions. Defense of cultural continuity. Opposition to a domestic left that views any expression of national identity as suspect. The LDP's dominance of Japanese politics for most of the postwar period reflects a country that, like America, has a durable conservative majority that the globalist left has never successfully displaced. The Abe-Trump relationship was not an accident of personal chemistry. It reflected something real. When Trump visited Japan in 2019, Abe organized a sumo tournament and a round of golf. They looked like two men who actually liked each other, because they did, because they understood each other's political project. Two leaders from two countries where the right had prevailed against a globalizing consensus that had declared nationalism obsolete. Then came July 8, 2022. Shinzo Abe was shot and killed while giving a campaign speech in Nara. The assassin was Tetsuya Yamagami, a man who had spent years consumed by a grudge against the Unification Church, which he blamed for destroying his family financially. He viewed Abe as the Church's most prominent political ally and targeted him for that reason. Yamagami later pleaded guilty to murder. The reaction in America, particularly on the right, was genuine grief. Abe wasn't just a foreign leader who had been friendly with Trump. He was understood as a kindred spirit, someone fighting the same cultural and ideological battle in his own country. The memes that followed said as much. After the Butler assassination attempt on Trump in July 2024, one of the most viral images on X was Abe's spirit reaching down from heaven to deflect the bullet. The joke was dark, but the feeling underneath it was real: American conservatives had genuinely mourned Abe, felt his loss personally, and the image of him protecting Trump from beyond captured something true about how the right in both countries saw each other. That kinship didn't disappear with Abe. Japan's current prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, is herself a Nippon Kaigi member and one of the most prominent figures in Japan's nationalist right. When she visited the White House in March 2026, the meeting was congenial and forward-looking. Then a Japanese reporter asked Trump why he hadn't briefed allied nations before the Iran strikes. Trump's answer was immediate: "Why didn't you tell ME about Pearl Harbor?" The chattering class erupted. Reckless. Offensive. Diplomatically disastrous. Takaichi smiled. Japan didn't take it as an insult, because it wasn't one. A Japanese citizen named captain S.O., writing on X the next day, put it better than any American commentator managed to: "Trump's Pearl Harbor joke wasn't an insult. It was the key that finally unlocked something buried deep in the Japanese soul. For 80 long years, we've carried" the weight of that defeat, of occupation, of being a nation that wasn't quite allowed to stand on its own. Trump's joke, directed at a Japanese reporter, sitting next to a Japanese prime minister, treated Japan as an equal, a country with its own complicated history that two adults could acknowledge and laugh about together. That's not how you talk to a vassal. That's how you talk to a friend. Both rights share something the international left cannot stand: the belief that nations are real, that cultures are worth preserving, that sovereignty is not a relic but a necessity. Both are in direct confrontation with movements that view national identity as inherently dangerous and cultural preservation as indistinguishable from chauvinism. The affinity that showed up on X last month is the popular expression of something that has been visible at the leadership level for years. WHERE IT GOES FROM HERE Japan is rearming, and this time it is not gradual or symbolic. In December 2022, Prime Minister Fumio Kishida announced a five-year defense buildup program targeting 2% of GDP in defense spending, a target previously associated with NATO membership requirements. Japan's fiscal year 2026 defense budget is on track to exceed $70 billion, making it one of the largest defense budgets in the world. The country has acquired Tomahawk cruise missiles from the United States, developing a counterstrike capability that would have been unthinkable under any previous interpretation of Article 9. The constitutional debate is no longer academic. Revision of Article 9 has majority support within the LDP and has moved from taboo to active political discussion. Japan is not yet a fully rearmed power, but the direction is unmistakable. A Japan that can project force changes the entire strategic geometry of Asia. South Korea, which has its own complicated history with Japan, has to recalculate. The Philippines, which is deepening its alliance with both the United States and Japan in response to Chinese pressure in the South China Sea, gains a more capable partner. Taiwan, whose survival depends on regional deterrence holding, gains another piece in a more credible defensive arrangement. For China, this is close to a nightmare scenario. Beijing's strategic calculation has long rested on the assumption that the American-led security architecture in Asia was fragile, dependent on American willingness to bear costs that domestic politics might eventually make unacceptable. A rearmed Japan with genuine offensive capability, embedded in a network of aligned regional partners who have stopped hedging between Washington and Beijing, changes that calculation significantly. The Pax Americana, in the form of a single hegemon guaranteeing everyone's security at American taxpayer expense, may indeed be contracting. What is replacing it is not a vacuum. It is a network of sovereign nations with aligned interests, capable of their own defense, choosing cooperation based on shared values rather than dependence on a single patron. That is not weakness. That is a more durable arrangement. WHAT CHINA IS WATCHING There is a reason China has been quiet about the American-Japanese social media moment, even as its state media works overtime to characterize every aspect of the US-Japan alliance as militarist aggression. Popular affinity between two democratic publics is exactly the kind of soft power that authoritarian systems cannot manufacture. The US-Japan alliance started as an occupation. It became a security arrangement. It became an economic partnership. It became something neither side fully planned for: a genuine friendship between two peoples with profoundly different histories, different languages, different cultures, who discovered, decade by decade and now post by post, that they see the world in compatible ways. What the right in both countries understands, and what the internationalist left has never quite grasped, is that alliances built on genuine affinity and shared values outlast alliances built on multilateral frameworks and bureaucratic process. NATO has a charter. The US-Japan alliance has something older and more durable: two peoples who have decided they like each other. China is watching. It should be paying attention.

SB19: P-Pop Kings Redefining Global Style

Photo Credits: 1Z Entertainment + Billboard Philippines + Mega Magazine + ITM. + VMan Southeast Asia

Origins: Forged in Fire

SB19 in school uniforms with umbrellas on grassy lawn 

In 2016, five young talents—Pablo Nase (leader), Josh Cullen Santos, Justin de Dios, Ken Suson, and Stell Ajero—entered a grueling survival show inspired by South Korean training camps. They endured physical drills, vocal bootcamps, and personality shaping under ShowBT Philippines, debuting as SB19 on October 26, 2018, with the heartfelt ballad "Tilaluha."

The early days were rocky. P-pop was nascent in the Philippines, and their debut barely registered amid K-pop's dominance. Yet, persistence fueled their spark—by 2019, explosive single "Go Up" ignited a movement, winning Song of the Year at the MYX Music Awards.
SB19 channels effortless charm on MEGA Magazine's cover, blending schoolboy whimsy with high-fashion edge.
